content.title: FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND LIKE {{MYTHS}} BUT AREN'T
facts: **Pineapple** actually eats you back — it contains bromelain, an enzyme so strong it breaks down proteins, which is why your tongue can feel raw after too much fresh pineapple.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange — the orange variety was bred centuries later, and the color has nothing to do with how much beta-carotene they contain.
**Almonds** are technically not nuts — they're seeds from inside a fruit that looks a lot like a peach, just with a leathery outer layer instead of soft flesh.
**Cashews** are never sold in their raw shell to consumers — the shell contains a toxic oil related to poison ivy, so every cashew you've ever eaten was steamed or roasted first.
**Nutmeg** contains a natural compound that can cause hallucinations in large doses — a few grams of ground nutmeg has been documented to trigger vivid, LSD-like effects.
**Watermelon** is over 90% water by weight — a single 300g slice can meaningfully contribute to your daily fluid intake, almost like drinking a glass of water.
**Chili peppers** don't actually burn your tongue — capsaicin binds to the same heat-sensing receptors triggered by actual high temperatures, tricking your brain into thinking you're being burned.
**Rhubarb** stalks are edible and tart, but its leaves contain enough oxalic acid to be genuinely toxic — one plant, two completely different safety profiles.

content.caption:
A few of these deserve more explanation than the image allows. Pineapple's bromelain enzyme doesn't just sit there — it's actively used in meat tenderizers and even some digestive supplements because it breaks down protein bonds just like it breaks down the proteins on your tongue's surface. Cashews go through a careful steaming process specifically to neutralize urushiol, the same irritant found in poison ivy, which is why you'll never find a truly raw cashew in stores. And nutmeg's hallucinogenic compound, myristicin, is metabolized by your liver into something structurally similar to certain psychoactive substances — which is exactly why more than a teaspoon or two is genuinely not a good idea. Bodies react differently to everything, so treat these as fascinating context, not a dosage guide.
